headline: Florida's early vote has turned Republican by registration, R+0.3 on 3.18 million ballots in the Oct 27 file (Republicans up 126,000 in person, Democrats up 116,000 by mail), still better for Democrats than R+5.3 at seven days out in 2022; the official same-point comparison across five states implies a national vote of about D-0.7 (±1.2) against 2022 and about D+5.0 (±1.6) against 2024, while the polls say D+8.8 and the app's forecast D+6.9. Nevada is D+5.5 against D+2.2 in 2022, Colorado D+7.9 against D+3.8, Iowa's absentee pool D+13.7 against D+22.4 and Pennsylvania's mail D+41.8 against D+51.0. The news comparisons lean Democratic: Jon Ralston's Nevada count reached D+24,395 (5.5 points) on Monday night with Clark's lead at 12.4 points against 7.9 at this stage in 2022, North Carolina is 36% ahead of 2022 with Republicans a quarter of in-person ballots, Texas's early vote is 74% ahead of 2022 with Democratic-primary voters now the larger group, and Wisconsin's returns have closed to 5% behind 2022.

measures.src: Florida Division of Elections daily file via the app's official comparison, Oct 27
measures.aff: Official data. 3,175,047 ballots in the Oct 27 file (mail 1,505,782, in person 1,669,265) vs. the state's figures at seven days out in 2024; 2024 is a presidential baseline in which Republicans had moved to in-person voting. Against 2022 the same file reads R+0.3 vs. R+5.3

measures.aff: Official data. 444,249 ballots through Oct 27's file (mail 263,414, in person 180,835) vs. Ralston's count at seven days out in 2024 (Republicans up 5.5); 2022 at the same point was D+2.2

measures.label: Colorado: returned ballots by registration, D-minus-R margin
measures.src: Colorado Secretary of State daily ballot-return release via the app's official comparison, Oct 26
measures.aff: Official data. 982,522 ballots through Oct 26 vs. 1,271,157 at eight days out in 2024; 2022 at the same point was D+3.8

measures.src: Iowa Secretary of State daily absentee report via the app's official comparison, Oct 27
measures.aff: Official data. 112,635 ballots received in the Oct 27 report vs. the state's report at the same point in 2024; 2022 at the same point was D+22.4, and Iowa Democrats vote absentee far more than Republicans in every year

measures.src: Pennsylvania Department of State daily mail-ballot report via the app's official comparison, Oct 26
measures.aff: Official data. 832,250 ballots returned through Oct 26 vs. about 1.43 million at the same point in 2024 (interpolated); no in-person early voting, and the mail pool is lopsidedly Democratic every year (D+51.0 at this point in 2022)

measures.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; affiliation not stated. 174,765 ballots through Oct 22 (Democrats 88,182, Republicans 36,939, unaffiliated 49,644) vs. the same point in 2024; vs. 2022 the gap is D+29.3 against D+29.9 with the count up 40%

measures.src: News 5 Cleveland, Oct 13 (Ohio Secretary of State data)

compare_note: Registered-party margin among early ballots, 2026 vs. the same point in 2024. Florida, Nevada, Colorado, Iowa and Pennsylvania are computed from the state files by the update job (Florida 3,175,047 ballots in the Oct 27 file against the state's 2024 figures at seven days out; Nevada 444,249 against Ralston's 2024 count; Colorado 982,522 through Oct 26; Iowa 112,635 absentees in the Oct 27 report; Pennsylvania 832,250 mail ballots through Oct 26); Maine is Call the Map's reading of the state file (174,765 ballots through Oct 22). Virginia's early voters are 63% Democratic on L2's modeled two-party split, vs. 59% at the same point in 2024 (Morris, Oct 12); Ohio's early voters were 41% Democratic and 28% Republican by last primary ballot as of Oct 13, vs. 26% and 36% at this point in 2024 (News 5 Cleveland, from Secretary of State data). Every state with party registration is more Democratic than at this point in 2024, Florida most of all because 2024's Republicans had moved to in-person early voting; against 2022 the official comparison is narrower and mixed (Florida R+0.3 vs. R+5.3, Nevada D+5.5 vs. D+2.2, Colorado D+7.9 vs. D+3.8, Iowa D+13.7 vs. D+22.4, Pennsylvania D+41.8 vs. D+51.0), and North Carolina's comparison is computed from the State Board's files.

bullets.title: The official comparison with 2022 covers five states and implies a national vote of about D-0.7; against 2024 it reads about D+5.0.
bullets.html: By registration, Florida's Oct 27 file counts 3,175,047 ballots at R+0.3 (mail 649,785 Democrats to 533,993 Republicans; in person 604,687 to 730,769), against R+5.3 at seven days out in 2022 (the state's Nov 1, 2022 figures); Nevada's 444,249 ballots are D+5.5 (mail D+30,113, in person R+5,719) against D+2.2 on the same day in 2022; Colorado's 982,522 returned ballots (Oct 26) are D+7.9 against D+3.8; Iowa's 112,635 absentees are D+13.7 against D+22.4; and Pennsylvania's 832,250 returned mail ballots (Oct 26) are D+41.8 against D+51.0. The app's calibrated slopes turn those into +4.2, +2.8, +3.4, -1.9 and -2.0 points of margin and a pooled implied national vote of about D-0.7 (±1.2), against polls at D+8.8 and the app's forecast at D+6.9; the Oct 26 files read D-1.1 on the same five states. Against 2024 the same files read better for Democrats: Florida R+0.3 against R+11.6 (worth about +9.5), Nevada D+5.5 against R+5.5 (+9.3) and Colorado D+7.9 against D+2.3 (+4.7) pool to about D+5.0 (±1.6); Pennsylvania's mail at D+41.8 against D+26.5 is worth about +3.4 (±3.4) and Iowa's D+13.7 against D+1.8 about +2.7 (±3.4). Arizona's county compilation reads R+0.7 on 971,184 ballots with no same-point baseline.
sources: Florida Division of Elections via the app's official comparison, Oct 27
UF Election Lab daily file (Nevada, Oct 27)
Pennsylvania Department of State daily mail-ballot report via the app's official comparison, Oct 26
CBS Miami/News Service of Florida, Oct 31, 2022 (the 2022 Florida baseline)

bullets.title: Nevada: Democrats' lead reached 24,395 ballots (5.5 points) Monday night; Clark is 12.4 points Democratic against 7.9 at this stage in 2022.
bullets.html: Jon Ralston's count at 10 p.m. Oct 26: 'D+24,395 (5.5 points), net D+3,943 so far today versus Sunday's final,' after a late Clark mail batch that ran 'almost 3-to-1 Ds' (5,539 ballots, D+2,940, R+1,073). At 9 p.m. almost 439,000 ballots had been cast, 21% of active voters and about 40% of an expected 1.1 million; 'Democrats lead Republicans in Clark by 36,784 ballots (12.4 points), compared with 20,880 (7.9 points) in 2022'; the in-person vote is D+4,643 'versus R+14,932 in 2022,' and the mail D+32,141 against D+35,812 then. Washoe was D+4,903 (5.8 points) on 84,064 ballots and the rurals R+18,111 (31.4 points) on 57,600. Sunday's final file read D+20,432 (5.2 points) on 395,325 ballots, with Clark 66.5% of the vote (66.8% in 2022's final), Washoe 20.2% (19%) and the rurals 13.3% (14.1%). Ralston writes that a 25,000-ballot statewide lead 'seems like a lock,' that under a 2022-based model Lombardo 'would need almost 51 percent of the votes left' and about 70% of the rurals, and that 'this weekend's Democratic wave has changed everything.' The state's Oct 27 file reads D+5.5 on 444,249 ballots against D+2.2 at this point in 2022 and R+5.5 in 2024.
sources: UF Election Lab daily file (Nevada, Oct 27)
bullets.aff: Nonpartisan outlet; county and Secretary of State data

bullets.title: North Carolina's early vote is 36% ahead of 2022 at nearly 1.6 million ballots; Republicans are a quarter of in-person ballots.
bullets.html: Michael Bitzer's Day 11 post (data through Sunday Oct 25): 'With nearly 1.6 million ballots cast (in-person and mail-in), the state is about half-a-million ballots away from exceeding the total cast in 2022,' and the count remains '36% ahead of where N.C. early voting was just four years ago.' Despite 23 counties cutting Sunday hours (scheduled site-hours down 23.5%), Sunday ballots rose 17.4% and the two weekends produced about 212,000 ballots against 150,000 in 2022, up 43%. 'Three-quarters of the in-person early ballots accepted are from registered Democrats and unaffiliated voters, while a quarter are from Republicans'; weekend voters were more unaffiliated and more racially diverse than in 2022, and voters under 46 were 35.1% of the two-weekend electorate against 27.5%. He expects 'slightly below/right at 3 million early ballots,' with Friday the biggest day. Call the Map's reading of the Oct 25 file: 1,583,182 ballots, Democrats 658,507 (up 44% on 2022), Republicans 373,431 (up 4%), unaffiliated 551,244 (up 59%), a D+18.0 gap against D+8.4; mail is 3.8% of ballots. The app's own file carries the official comparison.
sources: Call the Map (NC State Board of Elections file), Oct 26
bullets.aff: Nonpartisan academic; official data; Call the Map is an independent tracker

bullets.title: Georgia passed 1.78 million ballots entering the final week; TargetSmart models the early electorate 54% Democratic-aligned.
bullets.html: FOX 5 Atlanta's reading of the Secretary of State's data hub on Oct 26: 1,781,209 ballots accepted, 23.7% of 7,530,073 active voters; 1,698,469 in person and 82,740 accepted absentee ballots (164,750 requested, against more than 285,000 requests in all of 2022). The state's last same-point figure put in-person voting 12% ahead of 2022 as of Oct 20, and day one was 40% ahead. By race: 890,760 white voters, 544,112 Black, 46,132 Hispanic, 40,165 Asian or Pacific Islander; the largest age bands are 60-64 (213,257) and 65-69 (209,899). TargetSmart's model puts the early electorate at 54% Democratic-aligned, 41% Republican-aligned and 5% other. The AJC's county analysis (Oct 23) had the statewide count about 5% ahead of the same stage in 2022, the 27 Harris counties up 9% and the 132 Trump counties flat. Georgia has no party registration; early voting ends Oct 30.
sources: FOX 5 Atlanta (Secretary of State data hub), Oct 26
AJC (Greg Bluestein and Nicole Minshew), Oct 23
bullets.aff: Official data via nonpartisan outlets; TargetSmart is a Democratic-aligned vendor whose party figures are modeled

bullets.title: Texas: nearly 4.5 million voted in the first week, 74% ahead of 2022, and Democratic-primary voters outnumber Republican-primary voters for the first time.
bullets.html: The Texas Tribune (Oct 27): 'Nearly 4.5 million Texans' voted in the first seven days, 23.4% of a record 19 million registered voters, against 24.3% at the same point in 2018 and a pace above 2022's. Newsweek's reading of the Secretary of State's unofficial count through Oct 26: 4,538,667 ballots, 'up 74 percent compared with the same point in the 2022 midterm cycle.' Republican data analyst Derek Ryan's first five days: 36% of voters had a Democratic primary history and 35% a Republican one, about 25% none; Democratic-primary voters outnumbering Republican-primary voters at this stage is unprecedented, since Republican-primary voters had the larger share at this point in 2022 and 2024. Hispanic voters were 18% of the vote, 2 points above 2024 and 3 above 2022, and more than 2.1 million voters from the last four Republican primaries had not yet voted; Ryan expects 20-30% of all votes Wednesday through Friday and up to 10 million in all. theoelections' count through Oct 26: 4,555,567 voters; in-person ballots 32.7% from Democratic-primary-only voters and 32.6% Republican-only (31.6% neither), the mail 35.9% to 26.5%. Texas has no party registration.
sources: Newsweek (Texas Secretary of State data), Oct 27
bullets.aff: Nonpartisan outlets; Derek Ryan is a Republican consultant; theoelections is an independent tracker whose affiliation is not stated

bullets.title: Florida: the combined count turned Republican, R+0.3 in the Oct 27 file, with Republicans up 126,000 in person and Democrats up 116,000 by mail.
bullets.html: The Division of Elections' Oct 27 file (the app's official comparison) has 1,669,265 in-person ballots, 730,769 Republican to 604,687 Democratic (R+126,082), and 1,505,782 mail ballots returned, 649,785 Democratic to 533,993 Republican (D+115,792): 39.9% Republican to 39.5% Democratic on 3,175,047 ballots; the Oct 26 file was the first Republican reading of the year (R+0.4) after D+6.7 at twenty days out and D+0.3 on Oct 25. Monday's file (through Oct 25, per SignalData) had the mail at D+103,642 and the in-person vote at R+94,750. Call the Map reads the Oct 26 file as R+0.5 against R+4.5 on the same day of voting in 2022 and R+6.7 in 2022's final early vote, with ballots 4% ahead of 2022, Democrats up 7% and Republicans down 3%. At seven days out in 2022 the state was R+5.3 (the app's baseline from the state's Nov 1 figures, 3.30 million ballots), and at the same point in 2024 R+11.6.
sources: Florida Division of Elections via the app's official comparison, Oct 27
CBS Miami/News Service of Florida, Oct 31, 2022
bullets.aff: Official data; SignalData and Call the Map are independent trackers

bullets.title: Turnout without party: Wisconsin's returns have closed to 5% behind 2022, Pennsylvania's mail is 1% behind, Michigan is 16% voted, Maine 37% ahead.
bullets.html: Wisconsin: 377,058 absentee ballots returned (mail plus in person) against 397,174 at the same point in 2022, '20,116 ballots behind, or 5.1%,' narrowing from 10.4% the day before; in-person absentee ballots 148,896 since Oct 20; Milwaukee County 57,293 against 63,733 (down 10.1%), Dane 50,974 against 59,890 (down 14.9%), Madison down 21.3%, Waukesha up 2.4% to 39,530, Washington up 22% (Dairyland Sentinel, from Elections Commission data, Oct 23). Pennsylvania: 829,477 mail ballots returned through Oct 25, 1% below the same day of voting in 2022, Democrats 550,403 (down 9%), Republicans 203,111 (up 21%), unaffiliated 75,963 (up 10%); D+41.9 against D+51.8 (Call the Map). Michigan: 1,074,736 absentee ballots returned of 2,148,228 requested and 138,686 early in-person votes through Sunday, 16.4% of 7,408,638 active voters; Detroit's eight centers took 2,305 ballots Saturday against 1,897 on day one of 2024 (CBS Detroit, from the Secretary of State's dashboard, Oct 26); the AP's same-point analysis calls Michigan 'similar to its 2022 level.' Maine: 186,169 absentee ballots through Oct 25, up 37% on 2022, Democrats 93,254 (up 32%), Republicans 39,605 (up 28%), unaffiliated 53,310 (up 58%), D+28.8 against D+29.4; in-person absentee ballots are 51.3% of the total.
sources: Dairyland Sentinel (Wisconsin Elections Commission data), Oct 23
CBS Detroit (Michigan Secretary of State dashboard), Oct 26
bullets.aff: Official data via an independent tracker and news outlets; Dairyland Sentinel's analysis is by a former Republican legislator

bullets.title: Nationally, 30 million have voted, 12% ahead of 2022 in the day-aligned states, and Democrats' edge looks like 2022's.
bullets.html: UF Election Lab counted 31,465,330 ballots across 49 reporting jurisdictions on Oct 26 (the app's file); Call the Map's Oct 26 tally is 29,398,708 in 46 states, with the six states it compares day by day (North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Maine, Nevada, Iowa and Florida) 12% ahead of 2022 at the same point. The AP's same-point analysis has Texas up about 74% on 2022, Maine about 39%, Ohio about 30%, Iowa down about 6% and Michigan similar. Pluribus News (Oct 23): Michael McDonald's count in the 27 party-registration states about 46% Democrats to 30% Republicans, L2's modeled figures 49% to 34%, and L2's Paul Westcott saying Democrats had 'the same early-vote edge at this point in 2022'; nearly 60% of early voters are over 65. The shift from mail to in person continues: North Carolina's mail is 3.8% of ballots, Nevada's mail share is above 60% against about half in 2022, Florida's in-person vote is 53% of the total and Republican by 126,000, Wisconsin's in-person absentee votes are a rising share of a smaller total.
bullets.aff: L2 is a nonpartisan commercial vendor whose party figures are modeled in states without registration; Pluribus and the AP are nonpartisan

calendar_note: Kentucky's early in-person voting runs Oct 29-31; it is the last battleground opening. Closing dates: Maine's no-excuse absentee period Oct 29; Georgia, Texas, Nevada and Arizona Oct 30; North Carolina Oct 31 (3 p.m.); Michigan Nov 1; Nebraska's in-person early voting Nov 2. Pennsylvania's and Ohio's mail-ballot application deadlines are Oct 27. Pennsylvania and New Hampshire have no early in-person voting.
cast_at_note: Ballots counted (UF Election Lab, 49 jurisdictions reporting, state data as of Oct 23-27) when these comparisons were compiled; sets the automatic early-vote weight.
signals_verdict: The official same-point comparison with 2022 (Florida, Nevada, Colorado, Iowa and Pennsylvania) implies a national vote of about D-0.7 (±1.2): Florida is R+0.3 by registration in the Oct 27 file against R+5.3 at seven days out in 2022, Nevada D+5.5 against D+2.2, Colorado D+7.9 against D+3.8, Iowa's absentee pool D+13.7 against D+22.4 and Pennsylvania's mail D+41.8 against D+51.0; against 2024, Florida (R+0.3 vs. R+11.6), Nevada (D+5.5 vs. R+5.5) and Colorado pool to about D+5.0 (±1.6), so the early vote fits a Democratic year without confirming polls at D+8.8. The news comparisons are bluer: Ralston's Nevada count reached D+24,395 (5.5 points) Monday night with Clark 12.4 points Democratic against 7.9 at this stage in 2022, North Carolina runs 36% ahead of 2022 with Republicans a quarter of in-person ballots, Texas's early vote is 74% ahead of 2022 with Democratic-primary voters the larger group for the first time, while Florida's in-person vote is Republican by 126,000, Pennsylvania's mail trails 2022 and Wisconsin's returns are 5% behind. The next tests are how far Florida's Republican margin grows in the final four days of in-person voting, Nevada's last three days before early voting closes Oct 30, Michigan's first full week of in-person voting and Georgia's and Texas's closing surge through Oct 30.

signals.title: Nevada Democrats' lead reached 24,395 ballots (5.5 points) Monday night; Clark is 12.4 points Democratic against 7.9 at this stage in 2022
signals.value: Jon Ralston's count, 10 p.m. Oct 26: 'D+24,395 (5.5 points), net D+3,943 so far today versus Sunday's final,' after a late Clark mail batch 'almost 3-to-1 Ds' (5,539 ballots, D+2,940, R+1,073). At 9 p.m.: almost 439,000 ballots, 21% of active voters, about 40% of an expected 1.1 million; 'Democrats lead Republicans in Clark by 36,784 ballots (12.4 points), compared with 20,880 (7.9 points) in 2022'; in person D+4,643 'versus R+14,932 in 2022,' mail D+32,141 against D+35,812. Washoe D+4,903 (5.8 points) on 84,064 ballots; rurals R+18,111 (31.4 points) on 57,600. A 25,000-ballot lead 'seems like a lock'; under a 2022-based model Lombardo 'would need almost 51 percent of the votes left.'
signals.catch: Registration is not vote choice. The Democratic edge is the mail (Clark's mail by 24 points); the in-person vote is close and Republicans won Election Day 2022 by nearly 50,000 ballots. The final two days of early voting are usually the largest, and about 700,000 votes are still to come. The state's own Oct 27 file reads D+5.5 on 444,249 ballots against D+2.2 at this point in 2022 and R+5.5 in 2024 (the app's official panel).
signals.aff: Nonpartisan outlet (Jon Ralston); county and Secretary of State data

signals.title: North Carolina's early vote is 36% ahead of 2022 at nearly 1.6 million; Republicans are a quarter of in-person ballots
signals.value: Michael Bitzer's Day 11 post (through Sunday Oct 25): 'nearly 1.6 million ballots cast,' about half a million short of 2022's total early vote and '36% ahead of where N.C. early voting was just four years ago'; the two weekends produced about 212,000 ballots against 150,000 in 2022 (up 43%) even with 23 counties cutting Sunday hours. 'Three-quarters of the in-person early ballots accepted are from registered Democrats and unaffiliated voters, while a quarter are from Republicans'; voters under 46 were 35.1% of the weekend electorate against 27.5% in 2022. Call the Map's reading of the Oct 25 file: 1,583,182 ballots, Democrats 658,507 (+44% on 2022), Republicans 373,431 (+4%), unaffiliated 551,244 (+59%), D+18.0 vs. D+8.4.
signals.catch: Registration is not vote choice, and much of the Democratic surge is 2022 Election Day voters moving earlier. Republicans outvoted Democrats on Election Day 2022, and Bitzer expects the total to land 'slightly below/right at 3 million,' between 2022's 2.1 million and 2024's 4.4 million. The app's own file carries the official comparison.
signals.src: Michael Bitzer (Catawba College), Oct 26; Call the Map, Oct 26
signals.aff: Nonpartisan academic; official data; Call the Map is an independent tracker

signals.title: Georgia passed 1.78 million ballots entering the final week; Harris counties were 9% ahead of 2022, Trump counties flat
signals.value: FOX 5 Atlanta's reading of the Secretary of State's data hub, Oct 26: 1,781,209 ballots accepted, 23.7% of 7,530,073 active voters, 1,698,469 in person and 82,740 absentee; absentee requests (164,750) are well below 2022's 285,000. The state's last same-point figure had in-person voting 12% ahead of 2022 as of Oct 20. By race: 890,760 white, 544,112 Black, 46,132 Hispanic, 40,165 Asian or Pacific Islander. TargetSmart's model: 54% Democratic-aligned, 41% Republican-aligned. The AJC's county analysis (Oct 23): statewide about 5% ahead of the same stage in 2022, the 27 Harris counties up 9%, the 132 Trump counties essentially flat, Cobb and Gwinnett about 15%, Richmond 65%.
signals.catch: Georgia has no party registration, so the direction comes from geography and a Democratic-aligned vendor's model. Registration grew from 7.8 to 8.2 million, which lifts every county, and the electorate is old (the largest age bands are 60-69). Rick Jackson's campaign has been warning rural voters to turn out; early voting ends Oct 30.
signals.aff: Official data via nonpartisan outlets; TargetSmart is a Democratic-aligned vendor (modeled party)

signals.title: Texas: nearly 4.5 million voted in week one, 74% ahead of 2022, and Democratic-primary voters outnumber Republican-primary voters for the first time
signals.value: Texas Tribune (Oct 27): 'Nearly 4.5 million Texans' voted in the first seven days, 23.4% of 19 million registered (24.3% at the same point in 2018); Newsweek's reading of the Secretary of State's count through Oct 26: 4,538,667 ballots, 'up 74 percent compared with the same point in the 2022 midterm cycle.' Republican analyst Derek Ryan's first five days: 36% of voters with a Democratic primary history, 35% Republican, about 25% none; Democratic-primary voters outnumbering Republican-primary voters at this stage is unprecedented (Republican-primary voters led at this point in 2022 and 2024); Hispanic share 18%, 2 points above 2024. theoelections through Oct 26: in-person ballots 32.7% Democratic-primary-only, 32.6% Republican-only, 31.6% neither; mail 35.9% to 26.5%.
signals.catch: No party registration: 'party' is primary history, and 2022's electorate was unusually Republican. Ryan notes more than 2.1 million voters from the last four Republican primaries have not yet voted and expects 20-30% of all votes Wednesday through Friday; Mark Jones (Rice) warns of 'a tendency to over-interpret early vote numbers because we don't have good benchmarks.'
signals.src: Texas Tribune, Oct 27; Newsweek, Oct 27; theoelections, Oct 26
signals.aff: Nonpartisan outlets; Derek Ryan is a Republican consultant; theoelections is an independent tracker whose affiliation is not stated

signals.title: Florida's combined early vote has turned Republican by registration, R+0.3 in the Oct 27 file, with Republicans up 126,000 in person
signals.value: Division of Elections file for Oct 27 (the app's official panel): 1,669,265 in-person ballots, 730,769 Republican to 604,687 Democratic (R+126,082, from R+94,750 on Oct 25); 1,505,782 mail ballots returned, 649,785 Democratic to 533,993 Republican (D+115,792). Combined: 39.9% Republican to 39.5% Democratic on 3,175,047 ballots, after D+6.7 at twenty days out and D+0.3 on Oct 25; the Oct 26 file (R+0.4) was the first Republican reading of the year. Call the Map reads the Oct 26 file as R+0.5, with ballots 4% ahead of 2022, Democrats up 7% and Republicans down 3%.
signals.catch: The same-point comparison still favors Democrats: R+5.3 at seven days out in 2022 and R+11.6 in 2024 (the app's official panel), and 2022's final early vote was R+6.7. Republicans won Florida's in-person vote by far more in both years; the question is how far the margin grows in the last four in-person days. Registration is not vote choice.
signals.src: Florida Division of Elections daily file via the app's official comparison, Oct 27; Call the Map, Oct 26
signals.aff: Official data; Call the Map is an independent tracker

signals.title: Pennsylvania's mail returns trail 2022 by 1%, with Democrats' returns down 9% and Republicans' up 21%
signals.value: Call the Map (Oct 26 reading of the state file through Oct 25): 829,477 mail ballots returned, 1% below the same day of voting in 2022; Democrats 550,403 (down 9%), Republicans 203,111 (up 21%), unaffiliated 75,963 (up 10%); D+41.9 vs. D+51.8. The state's Oct 26 file: 832,250 returned; the app's official panel reads D+41.8 against D+51.0 at this point in 2022 and D+26.5 in 2024. Pluribus News (Oct 23) called Pennsylvania the only state where Democratic turnout trails the same point four years ago.
signals.catch: Pennsylvania's mail vote is lopsidedly Democratic every year (D+51 at this point in 2022, when Republicans won the national vote), and Democrats are shifting to Election Day voting after their own warnings about the mail; the state has no in-person early voting, so there is no in-person count to offset it. The official comparison is on the app's panel, so this signal is the turnout picture only. The mail application deadline is Oct 27.
signals.src: Call the Map, Oct 26; Pluribus News, Oct 23
signals.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; Pluribus News is a nonpartisan outlet

signals.title: Wisconsin's absentee returns trail 2022 by 5.1%, with Milwaukee down 10% and Dane down 15%
signals.value: 377,058 absentee ballots returned (mail plus in person) as of Oct 23 against 397,174 at the same point in 2022, '20,116 ballots behind, or 5.1%,' narrowing from 10.4% the day before (Dairyland Sentinel, from Elections Commission data); in-person absentee ballots 148,896 since Oct 20. Milwaukee County 57,293 vs. 63,733 (down 10.1%), Dane 50,974 vs. 59,890 (down 14.9%), Madison down 21.3%; Waukesha 39,530 (up 2.4%), Washington 12,489 (up 22%), the three WOW counties up 4.9% combined.
signals.catch: No party registration. Much of the decline is a mode shift away from mail that both parties encouraged, and in-person absentee voting runs through Nov 1, so the gap has been closing by about five points a day; Call the Map's civicAPI count (641,000 through Oct 26, 27% ahead of 2022) points the other way, so the basis matters. The analysis is by Joe Handrick, a former Republican legislator. The Democratic counties' declines are larger than the suburban Republican counties', which is the part that leans Republican.
signals.src: Dairyland Sentinel (Wisconsin Elections Commission data), Oct 23
signals.aff: Official data via a conservative-leaning Wisconsin news site; analysis by a former Republican legislator

signals.title: Michigan is 16% voted with 1.07 million absentee returns and 139,000 in-person votes; the AP's same-point read is 'similar to 2022'
signals.value: CBS Detroit's reading of the Secretary of State's dashboard, Oct 26: 1,074,736 absentee ballots returned of 2,148,228 requested (50%), 138,686 early in-person votes through Sunday, 16.4% of 7,408,638 active voters; Detroit's eight early-voting centers took 2,305 ballots Saturday against 1,897 on day one of 2024. The AP's analysis (via The National Desk) puts Michigan's early vote 'similar to its 2022 level' at the same point. The last numeric comparison (MITechNews, Oct 20): returns up 2.3% on 2022 while requests were up 17.2%.
signals.catch: Michigan has no party registration, so this measures turnout, not direction. About 94% of requests come from the permanent mail list, which inflates the request count and lowers the return rate. Statewide in-person early voting opened only Oct 24 and runs through Nov 1, so the same-point comparison will move this week.
signals.src: CBS Detroit (Michigan Secretary of State dashboard), Oct 26; The National Desk (AP), Oct 26; MITechNews, Oct 22

signals.title: Ohio's early electorate flipped from Republican to Democratic, and the AP has the state 30% ahead of 2022
signals.value: Democrats had returned about 94,000 ballots, unaffiliated voters a little more than 67,000 and Republicans nearly 64,000 (by last primary ballot), per the Ohio Capital Journal from Secretary of State data through Oct 12-13; News 5 Cleveland put Democrats at 41% and Republicans at 28% of nearly 230,000 early votes as of Oct 13, vs. 26% and 36% at this point in 2024. The AP's same-point analysis (Oct 26) has Ohio's early vote about 30% ahead of 2022; Call the Map counts 1.08 million ballots through Oct 25 (452,000 mail, 632,000 in person), without party.
signals.catch: 2024 was a presidential year, and Ohio Republicans are shifting from mail to later voting: mail requests were 631,079 vs. 871,041 at this point in 2022. 'Party' is the last primary ballot pulled; seniors are more than half of ballots. No newer party breakdown has been published since Oct 15.
signals.src: Ohio Capital Journal (Ohio Secretary of State data), Oct 15; The National Desk (AP), Oct 26

signals.title: Virginia's early vote is about 80% ahead of the comparable stage of 2022
signals.value: Nearly 930,000 Virginians had voted through Thursday Oct 22, 'about 80% more than at the comparable 2022 stage,' per Virginia Public Access Project data reported by The Hill (via IBTimes UK, Oct 24); Call the Map counts 942,000 through Oct 23 (261,000 mail, 681,000 in person). WTVR had more than 678,000 by Oct 18, nearly 300,000 ahead of the same point in 2022.
signals.catch: Virginia has no party registration, so this is turnout, not direction, and the 80% figure is secondhand (The Hill via IBTimes). Virginia's 2025 governor race already showed a Democratic swing, so high turnout here says less about the national picture. The modeled party lean is in the separate L2 measure.
signals.src: IBTimes UK (The Hill, VPAP data), Oct 24; Call the Map, Oct 26
signals.aff: Nonpartisan outlets; VPAP is a nonpartisan tracker of state data

signals.title: Maine's absentee vote is 37% ahead of 2022 with unaffiliated voters up 58%; the party gap matches 2022's
signals.value: 186,169 ballots through Oct 25 (Call the Map's reading of the Secretary of State file): Democrats 93,254 (up 32% on 2022), Republicans 39,605 (up 28%), unaffiliated 53,310 (up 58%); a D+28.8 gap vs. D+29.4 at the same point in 2022 (and D+17.9 at the same point in 2024 on the Oct 22 reading). In-person absentee ballots are 101,103 (51.3%) and mail 96,001.
signals.catch: Registration is not vote choice. Against 2022 the gap is half a point narrower, so the Democratic reading comes from turnout and the 2024 comparison, and the unaffiliated voters who decide the Collins race are the fastest-growing group. In-person absentee voting ends Oct 29.
signals.src: Call the Map (Maine Secretary of State absentee file), Oct 26
signals.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; affiliation not stated

signals.title: Clark County's mail vote is 6 points less Democratic than at this point in 2022
signals.value: Clark County mail ballots through Oct 24 (Call the Map): 142,921, up 7% on the same point in 2022; Democrats 63,642 (down 3%), Republicans 38,291 (up 14%), unaffiliated 40,987 (up 19%); a D+17.7 gap vs. D+24.1 at the same point in 2022. Ralston's statewide mail count Monday night: D+32,141 against D+35,812 at this point in 2022, with Clark's mail 'by 24 percentage points' on his county-wide figures.
signals.catch: Democrats are shifting from mail to in person, which Ralston's county-wide figures absorb (Clark overall is D+36,784, 12.4 points, against 7.9 in 2022); this compares only the mail mode, and mail is more than 60% of the vote this year against about half in 2022. Registration is not vote choice.
signals.src: Call the Map (Clark County mail file), Oct 26; Nevada Independent, Oct 26
signals.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; the Nevada Independent is a nonpartisan outlet

signals.title: L2: Democrats' national early-vote edge is the same as at this point in 2022
signals.value: Pluribus News (Oct 23): Michael McDonald's count in the 27 party-registration states about 46% Democrats to 30% Republicans, L2's modeled figures 49% to 34%, and L2's Paul Westcott says Democrats had 'the same early-vote edge at this point in 2022.' Nearly 60% of early voters are over 65. UF Election Lab's Oct 26 count is 31,465,330 ballots; Call the Map's six day-aligned states are 12% ahead of 2022, and the AP's same-point analysis has Texas up 74%, Maine 39%, Ohio 30%, Iowa down 6% and Michigan flat.
signals.catch: L2's party is modeled in states without registration, and the 2022 comparison is Westcott's characterization, not a published same-point table. Democrats' 2022 early-vote edge preceded a national vote they lost by about 3 points, which is why the edge alone says little; the turnout gains are concentrated in states whose Election Day vote was Republican in 2022.
signals.src: Pluribus News (Reid Wilson), Oct 23; The National Desk (AP), Oct 26; Call the Map, Oct 26
signals.aff: L2 is a nonpartisan commercial vendor (modeled party); McDonald is a nonpartisan academic
